lawyer:
HN Nandi, Advocate ----- For the Petitioner. 
Joya Bhartacharjee, Advocate ----- For the Opposite Party.
parties:
Mymensingh Arya Dharma Gnan Prodaini Sava ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Rabindra Narayan Paul ------ Opposite Party
full_judgment:
2. The petitioner as plaintiff instituted a suit for eviction of monthly tenant Brojendra Chandra Paul, the predecessor-in-interest of the opposite party, before the Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar Mymensingh being SCC Suit No.3 of 1985, on the ground of default in payment of rent and sub-letting a portion of the suit premises to an outsider beyond the knowledge and without the prior written permission of the landlord. It has been alleged that the defendant has been a monthly tenant in the suit premises at a monthly rent of Taka 40 only since 1962. In course of time, the defendant in a clandestine manner illegally inducted one Nirode Chandra Sarker as a sub-tenant in the suit premises beyond the knowledge of the landlord. It has been asserted that when the matter of sub-letting a portion of the suit premises to an outsider became known to the Secretary of the plaintiff, a meeting was convened on 10-8-1985 to discuss and consider the matter along with other matters and this meeting was attended by defendant Brojendra Chandra Paul. In that meeting Brojendra expressed his regrets for sub-letting a portion of the suit premises and proposed to pay an enhanced rent for the premises in question. In that meeting the rent was fixed at Taka 301 per month and an unanimous resolution of the Managing Committee was adopted on this question. This resolution Exhibit 1(Ka) was duly signed by defendant Brojendra showing his acceptance of the new rent but the defendant did not pay any rent in pursuance of the new agreement in spite of repeated demands by the landlord, as a result of which he became a defaulter in payment of rent. Thereafter by serving a notice upon the defendant under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, the tenancy in question was duly determined. The plaintiff has filed the present suit for eviction of the defendant on the ground of default in payment of rent and by sub-letting a portion of the suit premises to an outsider beyond the knowledge and against the consent of the plaintiff. 

 3. Defendant Brojendra contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material allegations of the plaint contending, inter alia, that he is not a defaulter. It has been alleged that defendant Brojendra paid Taka 16,000 to the plaintiff for construction of the suit premises for accommodation of his family and of his brother Dhirendra Chandra Paul. After half of the construction of the suit premises was complete, Dhirendra expressed his unwillingness to reside in the suit premises and dissociated himself from the contract. It has been alleged that it was then settled between the defendant and the Managing Committee of the plaintiff that out of Taka 16,000 paid to the plaintiff for the purpose of constructing the suit premises, Taka 40 per month would be deducted as monthly rent of the suit premises till it was fully adjusted. It was also stipulated between the parties that after the full adjustment of the aforesaid sum of Taka 16,000 the rent of the suit premises would be raised to Taka 80 per month. It has also been alleged that it was stipulated between the parties that the defendant would be at liberty to induct sub-lessee in the suit premises but, in fact, the defendant never inducted any sub-tenant therein. It has been contended by defendant Brojendra that he allowed Nirode Chandra Sarder to reside in a portion of the suit premises for some time on compassionate grounds, without receiving any pecuniary consideration, It has been asserted that the defendant, in good faith, put his signature in a blank paper on the representation of Santosh Kumar Ghosh as a representative of the plaintiff in the name of 2 meetings. The defence denied to have agreed to pay rent at the rate of Taka 301 per month since then. It has been asserted that the plaintiff filed the suit with false and frivolous allegations for making illegal gains. 

 7. Mr HN Nandi, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff petitioner, submits that the learned Senior Assistant Judge seriously erred in law in dismissing the suit without properly discussing and considering the material evidence on record and the same has occasioned failure of justice. The learned Advocate further submits that in the face of the clear evidence of sub-lessee Nirode Chandra Sarker deposing as PW 2 that he had been a sub-tenant under defendant Brojendra for 19 years on payment of rent to him and in view of the consistent evidence of other PWs and virtual admission of the contesting defendant of subletting a portion of the suit premises without any prior written permission of the landlord, the learned Senior Assistant Judge was manifestly wrong in not decreeing the suit on the ground of inducting sub- tenant in the suit premises and the same has occasioned failure of justice. The learned Advocate submits that even if the defence plea regarding adjustment of Taka 16,000 against monthly rent is assumed to be correct, still then the entire amount was fully adjusted much before the pronouncement of the judgment and, in that view of the matter, the defendant must be adjudged as a defaulter in payment of rent in respect of the suit premises and, as such, the learned Senior Assistant Judge was manifestly wrong in not decreeing the suit on the ground of default in payment of rent. 

 10. Himangshu Jyoti Ray as the Secretary of the plaintiff Durgabari Arya Dharma Gnan Prodaini Sava, deposed as PW 1. He stated in his evidence that defendant Brojendra had been a tenant in the suit premises at a monthly rental of Taka 40 since 1962. He stated that subsequently defendant Brojendra illegally inducted sub-tenant Nirode without the prior approval of the plaintiff. He went on to state that on query from Nirode, he came to learn that defendant Brojendra had inducted him in the suit premises at a monthly rental of Taka 200. Thereafter, defendant was called in a meeting of the Managing Committee of the plaintiff Dharma Sava on 16-6-1983, where the defendant expressed his regrets for his misdeed and begged to be excused. In that meeting the rent of the suit premises was mutually settled at Taka 301 per month and an unanimous resolution of the Managing Committee of the plaintiff was adopted and defendant Brojendra duly signed the said resolution signifying his acceptance of the new rent. The relevant resolution dated 16-6-1983 has been marked as Exhibit 1 and signature of defendant Brojendra therein has been marked as Exhibit 3(Ka). He further stated that since the defendant did not pay any rent to the plaintiff in spite of repeated demands, the plaintiff served a notice upon the defendant under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, Exhibit 2 determining the tenancy. He admitted that the defendant had paid to the plaintiff Taka 16,000 at the time of constructing the house. He denied that the defendant did not willingly sign Exhibit 1 but his signature was obtained on a blank paper fraudulently. 

 In cross-examination he re-affirmed that defendant Brojendra of his own volition put his signature in the resolution dated 16-6-1983 Exhibit 1. He stated that although there was no specific agenda for enhancement of the rent of the suit premises, the matter was taken up under the miscellaneous head and a resolution was duly adopted thereon. He refuted the defence suggestion that the defendant is not a defaulter and that he did not induct any sub-tenant in the suit premises. 

 11. PW 2 Nirode Chandra Sarker stated in his evidence that he had been a sub-tenant under Brojendra in respect of the suit premises. He stated that initially he paid rent @ Taka 50 per month and subsequently it was raised to Taka 200 per month. He further stated that later he came to learn that he was a sub-tenant under defendant Brojendra, who did not grant him any receipt against payment of rent. 

 In cross-examination he stated that Brojendra represented to him that he was not required to communicate with the plaintiff. He added that he used and occupied one room, one kitchen, one tube- well and a part of the suit premises. He further stated that for 3/4 years since 1970 he paid rent to Brojendra @ Taka 50 per month and thereafter it was raised to Taka 200 a month. He clearly stated in his evidence that he had been a sub-tenant under the defendant for 10 years. He refuted the defence suggestion that he was allowed to stay in the suit premises by defendant Brojendra for only 3/4 years on the ground of religious affinity. 

 12. PW 3 Jitendra Chandra Debnath, a member of the Executive Committee of the plaintiff, stated in his evidence that he was present at the meeting of the Managing Committee of the plaintiff held on 16-6-1983. He stated that the defendant was present in that meeting. He also stated that in that meeting the question of sub-letting by the defendant came up for discussion and rent of the suit premises was refixed at Taka 301 per month and an unanimous resolution on that behalf was duly adopted. He put his signature in the resolution Exhibit 1(Ka). He clearly stated that defendant Brojendra also put his signature in the resolution agreeing to the new arrangement in respect of rent. In cross-examination he stated that he was present when Brojendra put his signature in the resolution book. In reply to a defence suggestion, he stated that not only Brojendra but also his son were present at the meeting. 

 13. DW 1 Rabindra Narayan Paul stated in his evidence that his father Brojendra and uncle Dhirendra had entered into an agreement with the Managing Committee of the plaintiff in 1962, following which they paid Taka 3,000 to the plaintiff as a grant and they further paid Taka 16,000 to the plaintiff for construction of the suit premises for accommodation of the two families. He stated that after half of the construction work was complete, his uncle Dhirendra withdrew from the contract and demanded back his share of the money amounting to Taka 8,000, which he had earlier paid to the plaintiff. Thereafter, defendant Brojendra had alone to pay the entire money on the understanding that he would be at liberty to induct sub-tenant in the suit premises as it suited his convenience. It was decided between the parties that Taka 10,000 would be adjusted against rent @ Taka 40 per month and after the said money was fully adjusted, the rent would be raised to Taka 80 per month. He denied to have inducted any sub-tenant in the suit premises. He stated that his father Brojendra allowed his “গুরু ভাই” Nirode to stay in the suit premises for a few months on compassionate grounds. He denied that his father agreed to pay Taka 301 as monthly rent for the suit premises. He further stated that his father Brojendra did not sign the so called resolution dated 16-6-1983. He stated that the signature of his father was fraudulently obtained on a blank paper in the name of holding a meeting. He stated that all their papers relating to the suit premises had been lost. He went on to state that the money they had advanced was for construction of the suit house and it has not been fully adjusted as yet against rent. He asserted that they constructed pucca structures in the suit premises and, as such, they were not ejectable tenants. He denied the suggestion that they are habitual defaulters and they have illegally inducted a sub-tenant in the suit premises. In cross-examination he stated that Nirode had been in the suit premises for 2 years. 

 14. OW 2 Subodh Deb stated in his evidence that he knows the contending parties. He stated in his evidence that Nirode Babu was allowed to stay in the suit premises as a friend of defendant Brojendra and he was not a sub-lessee in the suit premises. He stated that the defendant has been residing in the suit premises since 1962 at a monthly rent of Taka 40, which was to be adjusted against the advance made by the defendant. He stated that it was stipulated between the parties that after the full adjustment was made, the rent would be raised to Taka 80 per month. In cross-examination he stated that he used to coach the son of Brojendra at their residence. 

 16. DW 4 Abdul Bari stated in his evidence that he knows the contending parties and he lives at a little distance from the suit premises. He stated that the plaintiff constructed the suit premises on receiving Taka 16,000 from the father and uncle of DW 1 Rabindra. He stated that the monthly rent was fixed at Taka 80 out of which Taka 40 would be adjusted against the advance made by the defendant. He stated that it was further stipulated between the parties that if the defendant incurred any expenses in respect of the suit premises, the same would also be adjusted against the advance. He further stated that Nirode was not a sub-tenant under defendant Brojendra, He stated that Nirode was allowed to stay in the suit premises by Brojendra as he happened to be a disciple of a common preceptor. In cross-examination he stated that defendant No. 1 was a student when he had been the lecturer of English in Akhtaruzzaman Memorial College. He stated that Brojendra used to visit him at his residence off and on. He admitted that he does not know Nirode. 

 18. This is all about the evidence on record. In this case certain things stand admitted. There is no dispute to the fact the defendant has been a monthly tenant under the plaintiff since 1962. There is also no dispute to the fact that notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was duly served upon the defendant, determining the tenancy. The case of the plaintiff is that, the defendant is a defaulter in payment of rent and he illegally inducted a sub-tenant in the suit premises without the prior permission of the plaintiff. No written agreement creating tenancy has been produced before the Court. It has, of course, been admitted by PW 1 that the defendant has been a tenant in respect of the suit premises since 1962, which is not disputed by the contesting defendant. The receipt of Taka 16,000 by the plaintiff is also an admitted fact. While the case of the plaintiff is that although defendant Brojendra was inducted in the suit premises at a nominal rent of Taka 40 but subsequently, the said rent was enhanced to Taka 301 on the basis of a mutual agreement of the parties. The defence disputes this fact seriously. It has been alleged that the signature of Brojendra in the disputed resolution dated 16-6-1983 showing acceptance of Taka 301 as monthly rent by Brojendra was by way of misrepresentation of facts. This resolution dated 16-6-1983 adopted unanimously by the Managing Committee of the plaintiff has been marked Exhibit 1. At least three of the PWs examined in the case were present at the time of passing the resolution. The signature of defendant Brojendra in the disputed resolution Exhibit 1 showing his agreement to the new rent is also an admitted fact. The contention of the defence is that this was obtained on misrepresentation of facts. In the facts of the case and the evidence on record, I do not find any cogent reason to hold that defendant Brojendra, a man of earthly prudence, put his signature on a blank piece of paper to be subsequently converted into a resolution. I find that rent was raised to Taka 301 in the meeting of the Managing Committee held on 16-6-1983 and defendant Brojendra was present in the meeting and put his signature in the resolution to that effect, Exhibit 1, indicating his concurrence to the new rate of rent at Taka 301 per month in place of Taka 40 only fixed about two decades ago. Be that as it may, it is an admitted fact that the defendant did not pay any rent to the plaintiff at any point of time, except paying Taka 16,000 as an advance towards construction of the suit premises. The learned Senior Assistant Judge found in this impugned judgment that the defendant has been a tenant in respect of the suit premises since 1st January, 1962 and Taka 11,080 was adjusted against monthly rent @ Taka 40 till filing of the suit on 1-7-1985 and there remains a balance of Taka 4920 as unadjusted advance and, as such, the defendant cannot be found to be a defaulter. Even if the case of defendant is taken it its entirety, it is found that on the date of the judgment on 16-7-1990 the defendant's arrear rent dues to the plaintiff comes to Taka 6240 even @ Taka 40 per month. In that view of the matter, the entire advance made by the contesting defendant was fully adjusted long ago, there being admittedly no further payment of rent by the defendant to the plaintiff on any account whatsoever. 

 19. Section 10 of the East Pakistan Premises Rent Control Ordinance, which was in force when the disputed tenancy came into existence, prohibited any payment of advance for more than one month. The parties to the agreement appear to have acted against it and made an arrangement for adjustment of the monthly rent against the advance. Subsequently, Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963 and Premises Rent Control Act, 1991 (Act No. 111 of 1991) made similar provisions. Section 10 of the present Act makes an agreement for advance payment of rent beyond one month void. If any advance beyond one month's rent is received by the landlord, the tenant is entitled under section 16 of the Act to make an application within 6 months to the Rent Controller and in that case the Rent Controller may order refund of the advance rent or adjust any sum so paid or deposited in any other manner. Be that as it may, in the facts of the case, it is difficult to conclude with any amount of certainty that the defendant was a defaulter in payment of rent on the day of institution of the suit, in view of the novel arrangement made by the parties regarding payment of rent. 

 20. Now the question that calls for determination by this Court is, whether the plaintiff has been able to prove its allegation that the defendant illegally inducted a sub-lessee in the suit premises without the prior approval in writing of the plaintiff. From the evidence on record, I find that induction of sub-lessee Nirode Chandra Sarker in the suit premises by defendant Brojendra is virtually an admitted fact. The defence plea that Nirode was allowed to live in a portion of the suit premises for 3/4 years merely on humanitarian consideration has not been proved at all and, on the other hand, it has been proved by the most consistent and corroborative evidence of competent witnesses that defendant Brojendra illegally sub-let a portion of the suit premises to Nirode in a portion of the suit premises and realised monthly rent from him at varying rates. The evidence of PW 2 Nirode Chandra, a thoroughly independent and natural witness, fully corroborated by the three other PWs and virtually admitted by the defence, unmistakably proves that defendant Bojendra inducted sub-tenant Nirode in a portion of the suit premises without the prior written permission of the landlord and realised rent from the said sub-tenant for years. The evidence of the DWs on this point is widely discrepant and totally unconvincing. I, therefore, have no hesitation in finding that defendant Brojendra illegally inducted a sub-lessee in the suit premises without the prior written approval of the plaintiff and grossly violated the terms of the tenancy agreement and thereby rendered himself as an undesirable tenant, causing the plaintiff landlord serious prejudice. The defence plea that defendant Brojendra had an oral agreement with the plaintiff authorising him to induct a sub-lessee in the suit premises but, in fact, he did not do so, but simply allowed Nirode to reside in the suit premises with the members of his family on gratis for a few years, is not only a contradictory stand but the same has also been disproved by convincing evidence on record. The defendant is thus found to have illegally inducted a sub-lessee in the suit premises in flagrant violation of the agreement for the tenancy and made himself liable to be adjudged as an undesirable tenant. In the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record, I am of the firm view that the defendant offended the provision of section 17(1)(b) of erstwhile East Pakistan Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1961 which was in operation at the time of creation of the disputed tenancy in 1962, by sub-letting a portion of the suit premises to an outsider without the prior written consent of the landlord. Similar provision has been made in section 18(1)(b) of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963 and section 18(1)(b) of the Premises Rent Control Act, 1961. In any view of the matter, the defendant must be found to have grossly violated the tenancy agreement by sub-letting a portion of the suit premises to a stranger for financial considerations against the consent of the plaintiff landlord and, indeed, made himself an undesirable tenant. It is unfortunate that the learned Assistant Judge failed to apply his judicial mind into the facts and circumstances of the case and the material evidence on record and fell in error in reaching his conclusions on a superficial view of law and fact. The approach of the learned Assistant Judge to this vital legal aspect of the case is deprecated. 

 23. While parting with the case records, I think it necessary to mention that a tenant is under a legal obligation to pay rent regularly to the landlord and this alone can save him from ejectment. A tenant has no right to claim adjustment of any advance that he might have made to the landlord, against monthly rent, as advance rent or any premium in any form is strictly prohibited by law. Such an agreement is void and consequently, not conformable. The remedy for the tenant in a case of advance is to move the Rent Controller within 6 months of the creation of the tenancy for getting an order of refund or any adjustment as may be found just and proper. The tenant cannot avoid the mischief of ejectment in an action by the plaintiff on the plea that since he has made an advance to the landlord, he cannot be adjudged as a defaulter for non payment of rent till the advance was fully adjusted. I get instant support of this view in the case of Shamsuddin Ahmed vs Mohd Hossain reported in 31 DLR (AD) 155.
